extras.title: Nobatia
extras.location: Lower Nubia; southern Egypt and northern Sudan
extras.note: Christianised in the sixth century; later governed with Makuria while retaining a distinctive regional administration. Exact dates and circumstances of union are uncertain.

extras.title: Makuria
extras.location: Middle Nile; capital at Old Dongola
extras.note: Christian Nubian kingdom with changing territorial reach and late fragmentation; its chronology is not the lifetime of all Nubian communities.

extras.title: Alodia / Alwa
extras.location: Blue and White Nile region; capital at Soba
extras.note: Christian Nubian kingdom distinct from Makuria. Late chronicles associate Soba’s destruction with 1504, while archaeology indicates much earlier decline in excavated areas; a precise end date is uncertain.

extras.title: Funj Sultanate of Sennar
extras.location: Middle Nile and Blue Nile; changing dominions
extras.note: A regional sultanate conventionally dated from 1504. It incorporated diverse communities and territories and was not a restored, unchanged Alodian monarchy or all of modern Sudan.

extras.title: Turco-Egyptian Sudan
extras.location: Sudanese territories ruled from Egypt; frontiers changed
extras.note: Muhammad Ali’s conquest began in 1820, ending Funj rule in 1821. Egyptian government expanded unevenly into other regions; this did not constitute simultaneous control of every part of today’s Sudan and South Sudan.

extras.title: Mahdist State
extras.note: The movement began in 1881 and captured Khartoum in 1885. Omdurman fell in 1898; the Khalifa was defeated and killed in 1899. The stages should not be collapsed into a single founding or ending day.

extras.title: Anglo-Egyptian Sudan
extras.location: Territories of present-day Sudan and South Sudan, with changing boundaries
extras.note: The 1899 agreements established nominal joint British and Egyptian authority, with British officials dominant in administration. Colonial borders and institutions differed from those of preceding kingdoms.

extras.title: Sudan: independent eras
extras.note: An overview of successive governments and conflicts following independence, not one unchanged regime. South Sudan became independent in 2011; Sudan continued as a state. Ancient Nubian kingdoms were not coterminous with this modern country.

extras.title: South Sudan: independent state
extras.note: Independence on 9 July 2011 followed a January referendum under the 2005 peace settlement. This date marks a modern state, not the beginning of the histories of its many peoples.

maps.title: Sudan and South Sudan: kingdoms, conquest and independence

connections.label: Context: later Nubian kingdoms
connections.summary: After Meroe’s decline, several kingdoms developed in the Nubian Nile region.
connections.note: Context link, not a documented division of one empire into three states or an assertion of unchanged institutions; Christianisation followed during the sixth century.

connections.label: Nobatia and Makuria united
connections.dates: By the early medieval period · precise date uncertain
connections.summary: Nobatia came under a ruler shared with Makuria, while retaining regional institutions.
connections.note: The date and circumstances are uncertain; this does not imply that Alodia joined them.

connections.label: Context: changing regional rule
connections.summary: The Funj sultanate rose in the central Nile region after the decline of Alodian authority.
connections.note: Context, not a secure direct succession: later chronicles associate Soba’s destruction with 1504, but the excavated city shows earlier decline, and the chronology and agents of the political transformation remain disputed.

connections.label: Egyptian conquest ends Funj rule
connections.summary: Forces sent by Muhammad Ali conquered the Funj sultanate and established Egyptian administration.
connections.note: This was conquest and new colonial government, not a peaceful dynastic inheritance; control over other Sudanese territories expanded at different times.

connections.label: Egyptian territorial expansion
connections.summary: Muhammad Ali’s Egyptian government sent armies south and imposed rule over Sudanese territories.
connections.note: The Egyptian dynasty operated within a changing Ottoman imperial framework; the term Turco-Egyptian does not imply all inhabitants were Turkish or Egyptian.

connections.label: Mahdist revolt and capture of Khartoum
connections.summary: The Mahdist movement defeated Egyptian government forces and captured Khartoum in January 1885.
connections.note: The revolt began before the capture; Egyptian and British forces retained some peripheral positions, and not every community supported the Mahdist government.

connections.label: Anglo-Egyptian conquest
connections.summary: British-led Anglo-Egyptian armies defeated the Mahdist state, and the 1899 agreements established joint colonial rule.
connections.note: The decisive defeat at Omdurman occurred in 1898; fighting continued into 1899, so military conquest and the legal creation of the condominium are distinct stages.

connections.label: British-led colonial administration
connections.summary: Sudan was administered under a formal Anglo-Egyptian condominium in which British authority predominated.
connections.note: This was legally distinct from simply annexing Sudan as an ordinary British colony; Egyptian claims and participation persisted.

connections.label: Sudan becomes independent
connections.summary: Sudan became independent of the Anglo-Egyptian condominium.
connections.note: The independent state initially included the territory that later became South Sudan; independence did not resolve internal conflicts or guarantee one continuous constitutional order.

connections.label: South Sudan secedes after referendum
connections.summary: South Sudan became an independent state after the January 2011 referendum.
connections.note: Sudan continued as a state after the separation; this was not the replacement of Sudan by South Sudan, and it does not imply that all boundary questions were resolved.

editorialNotes: Selected Middle Nile pathway only: this map does not cover every Sudanese region, Darfur, all southern peoples, or every modern regime.
Render Context links dashed; they mark regional historical setting rather than direct political succession.
Do not label Alodia’s ending as a securely established Funj conquest in 1504; archaeological evidence complicates that late chronicle account.
